title: Coastal Brew
sub: Why is a growing coffee chain making less money?
skills: Reading a P&L · unit economics · cannibalisation
prompt: Our client, Coastal Brew, runs 120 coffee shops across the south of England. Over the last two years revenue has grown slightly, from $96M to $98M, but operating profit has fallen from $12M to $4.5M. The CEO has asked us to find out why profits are falling and what to do about it.

clarify.a: Company-owned cafés (no franchising). Sells hot drinks, cold drinks and food. Since 2024 it has also sold through two delivery apps.
Get back to at least $10M operating profit within two years.
Competitors report flat to slightly lower margins, nothing like a 60% drop. This is mostly a Coastal Brew problem.
No. 120 stores throughout, no openings or closures.

hypothesis: Revenue is roughly flat, so the problem is on the cost side, probably a new or fast-growing cost line. The delivery channel launched in this period, so that's where I'd look first.

questions.q: Here is the P&L. Where is the profit going?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Coastal Brew P&L
exhibit.note: Delivery orders were 5% of revenue in 2024 and 25% in 2026.

questions.answer:
Revenue added $2.0M, but costs rose by $9.5M. Two lines explain almost all of it:

  • App commissions: +$6.0M (from 1.5% to 7.6% of revenue). Delivery went from 5% to 25% of sales, and the apps charge ~30% commission.
  • Ingredients & packaging: +$2.5M, rising faster than revenue (25.0% → 27.0%), which points to delivery packaging.

Staff and rent are flat as a % of revenue. So-what: the delivery channel is eating the margin. Next I'd like to compare the profit on a delivery order with an in-store order.
questions.note: A strong candidate converts the cost lines into % of revenue without being asked.

questions.q: Compare the economics of an in-store order and a delivery order. Is delivery adding profit?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 2 · Order economics
exhibit.note: Customer research: 60% of delivery customers say they would otherwise have visited the café.

questions.answer:
Contribution per order (before staff, rent and overheads):

  • In-store: $6.00 − $1.50 = $4.50 (75%)
  • Delivery: $9.00 − $2.25 − $0.90 − $2.70 = $3.15 (35%)

But 60% of delivery orders replace an in-store visit. The true gain per delivery order = $3.15 − 0.6 × $4.50 = $3.15 − $2.70 = $0.45.

So-what: each delivery order looks bigger, but it adds only about $0.45 of profit because most of it replaces a high-margin café visit. The growth of delivery has mostly moved customers to a worse channel.
questions.note: Push weaker candidates: 'Is the $3.15 all new profit?' The cannibalisation step is what this case tests.

questions.q: What could Coastal Brew do to restore profit? Brainstorm.
questions.answer:
Make delivery orders more profitable

  • Charge higher menu prices on the apps (common practice)
  • Negotiate commission down in return for volume or exclusivity
  • A delivery-only menu built around high-margin items; cheaper packaging

Shift customers to cheaper channels

  • Own app with click-and-collect (no commission), with loyalty points to make the switch worth it
  • In-store offers aimed at customers who used to visit

Fix the base

  • Check staff scheduling against the lower in-store footfall

questions.q: The CEO likes the idea of raising delivery prices by 15%. The apps estimate we'd lose 10% of delivery orders. What's the impact? (We sell about 2.7M delivery orders a year.)
questions.answer:
New ticket $10.35; commission 30% = $3.11; ingredients $2.25 (same food); packaging $0.90.
New contribution = $10.35 − $3.11 − $2.25 − $0.90 ≈ $4.10 (up from $3.15).

Before: 2.7M × $3.15 ≈ $8.5M. After: 2.43M × $4.10 ≈ $10.0M. Gain ≈ $1.5M a year.

Sanity check: +$0.95 per order on 2.4M orders ≈ $2.3M, minus ~270k lost orders × $3.15 ≈ $0.85M, so ≈ $1.5M. ✓
Bonus point: some lost delivery customers may come back to the café, which makes the move even better.

reco: Coastal Brew's profit has fallen $7.5M because delivery has grown from 5% to 25% of sales, and a delivery order adds only ~$0.45 of real profit once you account for café visits it replaces. I recommend three moves: (1) raise app menu prices ~15%, worth about $1.5M a year; (2) launch click-and-collect in the Coastal Brew app to move customers off the commission channels; (3) renegotiate commissions with the threat of lower volume. Risk: the apps may rank us lower in search. Next step: test the price increase in 10 stores for 4 weeks before rolling it out.
great: Converts the P&L into % of revenue straight away
Spots cannibalisation without a hint
Sanity-checks the $1.5M a second way
Recommendation opens with the answer and the number, not a recap

title: Nordwind E-Bikes
sub: Should a Danish premium e-bike maker enter the US?
prompt: Nordwind makes premium e-bikes in Denmark and sells them through 600 bike shops across Europe (revenue $150M). European growth is slowing, so the founders are considering the United States. Their goal: $40M of US revenue within five years, and an operating profit in the US by year 3. Should they enter, and if so, how?

clarify.a: Premium city and trekking e-bikes, average retail price about $4,000.
Through independent bike shops. Nordwind sells to shops at 60% of retail price.
None today. A few US shops import small volumes informally.

structure.root: Should Nordwind enter the US, and how?

branches.head: How to enter?
items: Distributor vs own network vs acquisition

hypothesis: The US market is big enough. The real question is whether Nordwind can reach enough shops fast enough, so I expect the entry mode to decide the case.

questions.q: Here is some market data. What market share would Nordwind need to hit its goal in year 5?
questions.answer:
Year-5 market = 1.0M × 1.1⁴ ≈ 1.46M units → premium = 15% ≈ 220k units.

Units needed = $44M ÷ $2,400 ≈ 18,300 bikes → share of premium ≈ 18.3k ÷ 220k ≈ 8%.

So-what: 8% would make Nordwind roughly the #4 premium brand within five years. That's ambitious but not crazy in a fragmented segment. Next I'd look at the competition.

questions.q: Here are the premium competitors. What does this tell you?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 2 · US premium e-bike share of units, %

questions.answer: The market is fragmented: the top four hold 55% and a long tail holds 45%. A European brand (B) already holds 15%, so US buyers clearly accept European premium bikes. To reach 8%, Nordwind needs to match Brand D. So-what: the share target is realistic if Nordwind gets its bikes into enough shops. That makes the route to market the key decision.

questions.q: Nordwind is choosing between two ways to enter. Which is better?

rows: Variable cost per bike (make, ship, duty)
exhibit.title: Exhibit 3 · Entry options

questions.answer:
Contribution per bike: A = $2,400 × 85% − $1,500 = $540; B = $2,400 − $1,500 = $900.

Annual profit is the same when 540V − 1.5M = 900V − 6M → 360V = 4.5M → V = 12,500 bikes/year.

Below 12,500 bikes a year the distributor is better; above it, the own network wins. At year-5 volume (18,500): A = $8.5M, B = $10.65M.

Own-network breakeven = $6M ÷ $900 ≈ 6,700 bikes/year. If volumes ramp 3k → 7k → 11k → 15k → 18.5k, B makes a small profit in year 2, but recovering the $12M upfront takes until year 5.
questions.note: Let the candidate set up the indifference equation. Good candidates realise the answer is 'distributor first, then switch'.

questions.q: What risks should the founders weigh?
questions.answer:
• Tariffs and trade policy on EU-made goods can wipe out the $900 margin overnight. Consider US final assembly.
  • Distributor lock-in: a 5-year exclusive contract would block the switch to an own network.
  • Brand awareness: no US brand recognition, so early volumes may be slower.
  • Service: e-bikes need repairs and spare parts; shops need training.

reco: Yes, enter the US, but through a distributor first. Hitting $40M needs about 8% of the premium segment, which is achievable in a fragmented market. A distributor is more profitable until volumes pass ~12,500 bikes a year and needs no $12M upfront, so it also meets the 'profitable by year 3' goal more safely. The contract should be 3 years or less, with the right to take over distribution once that volume is reached. Main risk: tariffs. As a next step, model US assembly and start in 2-3 bike-friendly states.
great: States the 8% share and judges whether it's realistic
Sets up the 12,500-bike crossover clearly
Recommends a sequence (distributor → own network), not just one option
Raises tariffs without prompting

title: Meridian Hospitals
sub: How can a hospital chain double its revenue in five years?
skills: Revenue trees · sizing growth levers · capital constraints
prompt: Meridian runs 12 private multi-specialty hospitals in South India with revenue of $300M a year. The board wants to double revenue to $600M within five years without hurting quality. How should Meridian get there?

clarify.a: Inpatient 65%, outpatient consultations 20%, pharmacy 10%, diagnostics 5%.
2,400 beds. Average bed occupancy 62%; well-run peers in the region reach 75%.
EBITDA margin 18% (~$54M). Moderate debt; the board is open to raising more.
Mostly large cities (Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad). No presence yet in smaller (tier-2) cities.

hypothesis: Existing hospitals can deliver maybe a third of the growth through occupancy. The rest needs new beds, and given the 5-year time frame, buying hospitals may beat building them.

questions.q: Occupancy varies a lot by hospital. What do you see?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Bed occupancy by hospital, %
exhibit.note: H10-H12 opened in the last 3 years in newer parts of the cities.

questions.answer: Nine hospitals sit between 60% and 78%. Three newer ones (H10-H12) are around 40% and drag the average down to 62%. So-what: the occupancy problem is concentrated. Typical causes for new hospitals: not enough well-known doctors, and few referrals from local GPs. Fixing these three is the fastest growth lever available.

questions.q: How much revenue would Meridian gain by raising average occupancy from 62% to 75%?
questions.answer:
Inpatient revenue = 65% × $300M = $195M. Assuming revenue grows in line with occupied beds: $195M × 75/62 ≈ $236M → +$41M.

If the other streams (outpatient, pharmacy, diagnostics: $105M) grow ~10% a year organically: $105M × 1.1⁵ ≈ $169M → +$64M.

Existing hospitals ≈ +$105M. Gap still to fill ≈ $195M. So-what: around two-thirds of the target needs new capacity.

questions.q: Here are two ways to add capacity. How would you fill the remaining $195M?
questions.answer:
A hospital built in year 1 only matures in year 5, so building alone is too slow: ~5-6 new hospitals ($200-240M) all opened in year 1.

Buying gives revenue straight away: about 4 acquisitions at ~$35M each after upgrade ≈ $140M for ~$150M. Add 2 new builds in big cities for ≈ $55-70M by year 5 → total ≈ $195-210M.

Funding: ~$230M over 5 years against ~$54M+ a year of EBITDA. Doable with some debt, but tight. Look at asset-light options (management contracts) to reduce the capital needed.

reco: Meridian can reach $600M, but it can't build its way there in five years. I recommend three steps: (1) fix the three under-filled hospitals and lift occupancy to 75% (+~$40M), alongside organic growth in outpatient, pharmacy and diagnostics (+~$65M); (2) buy about four hospitals in tier-2 cities (+~$140M), which also opens new markets; (3) build two flagship hospitals in big cities (+~$60M by year 5). Total investment is about $230M. The biggest risk is keeping quality consistent across acquired hospitals, so next steps are a clinical-quality checklist for acquisitions and a shortlist of targets.
great: Sizes each lever, adds them up, and names the remaining gap
Notices that new builds take 4 years to mature
Checks whether the plan can be funded
Mentions quality, the client's own constraint

title: PackRight
sub: Should a packaging maker buy a plastics recycler?
skills: Valuation with multiples · synergies · avoiding double counting
prompt: PackRight makes plastic packaging for food and drink brands across Europe: revenue $800M, EBITDA $120M. New rules will require packaging to contain at least 30% recycled plastic by 2030. PackRight is considering buying RePlast, a recycler with revenue of $100M and EBITDA of $12M. The owners are asking $180M. Should PackRight buy?

clarify.q: Why buy, not buy on the market?
clarify.a: PackRight worries it won't be able to buy enough recycled plastic at a reasonable price.
Uses 400,000 tonnes of plastic a year → needs 120,000 tonnes recycled by 2030.
80,000 tonnes a year, sold at market price (~$1,500/tonne) to many buyers.
Recyclers usually sell for 9-11× EBITDA. Use 10×.

structure.root: Is RePlast worth more than $180M to PackRight?

branches.head: Deal
items: Alternatives: long-term contracts, build our own plant

hypothesis: At 15× EBITDA the asking price is high for a recycler. I expect the deal to make sense only if the supply-security benefit is real and large.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · European recycled plastic, million tonnes (case data)

questions.answer: Supply exceeds demand until 2027. From 2028 demand overtakes supply, and by 2030 the gap is 1.9Mt (−20%). So-what: recycled plastic will be scarce just as PackRight legally needs it. Expect prices to rise, and some buyers to get no supply at all. Securing supply is valuable.

questions.q: A colleague says: 'RePlast's plastic costs $1,200/tonne to make and sells for $1,500. If we own it, we save $300 × 80,000 = $24M a year. That's a huge synergy.' Do you agree?
questions.answer:
No, that's double counting. RePlast already earns that $300/tonne margin. It's part of the $12M EBITDA we're paying for. Moving the profit from RePlast to PackRight doesn't create new profit for the group.

The real value is access: in a shortage, owning RePlast guarantees 80k of the 120k tonnes needed, and protects PackRight against price spikes and lost contracts.
questions.note: This is the key test of the case. Don't hint unless the candidate is completely stuck.

questions.q: Now value the deal. Real synergies: $5M a year of cost savings (logistics, overheads), and brands will pay a 5% premium for guaranteed-recycled packaging on $200M of PackRight sales, about $6M of extra EBITDA. Integration costs $15M one-off.
questions.answer:
RePlast standalone: 12 × 10$120M
Cost synergies: 5 × 10$50M
Revenue synergies: 6 × 10$60M
Integration cost−$15M
Maximum value to PackRight$215M

$215M > $180M asking → $35M of value created. But without the revenue synergy: 120 + 50 − 15 = $155M < $180M.

So-what: the whole decision depends on whether customers really pay the green premium, which is the least certain synergy.

questions.q: How would you protect PackRight in the deal?
questions.answer:
• Negotiate the upfront price towards ~$155-165M (what's justified without the revenue synergy)
  • Pay an earn-out (extra payment later) only if green-premium contracts are signed
  • Before signing, get letters of intent from 2-3 major brands for the premium packaging
  • Check RePlast's technology can produce food-grade recycled plastic

reco: PackRight should buy RePlast, but not at a flat $180M. Recycled plastic will be scarce from 2028, and RePlast covers two-thirds of what PackRight legally needs by 2030. With all synergies, RePlast is worth about $215M to PackRight. Without the uncertain green premium, it's worth only $155M. So I'd offer around $160M upfront plus an earn-out of up to $20M tied to signed premium contracts. Key risk: integration and food-grade quality. Next steps: technical due diligence and talks with three anchor customers.
great: Catches the $24M double count
Separates certain synergies from uncertain ones
Structures the price (earn-out) instead of giving a plain yes or no
Connects the regulation deadline to the shortage

title: FitHub Gyms
sub: Should a private equity fund buy a budget gym chain?
skills: LBO-style returns maths · value creation plan · exit
prompt: Summit Capital, a mid-sized private equity fund, has been offered FitHub, a chain of 80 budget gyms in the UK. FitHub makes $25M EBITDA and the seller is asking 8× EBITDA ($200M). Summit needs to make 2.5× its money within five years. Should Summit invest?

clarify.a: 50% debt, 50% fund equity: $100M debt, $100M equity.
Sell in year 5 at the same 8× multiple. Debt expected to fall to $60M by then from cash flow.
~4,000 members per gym, $25/month, no contract. Gyms are leased.
UK budget gyms growing ~5% a year; two large competitors.

hypothesis: Work backwards: figure out the EBITDA FitHub needs in year 5, then check whether the plan gets there.

questions.q: What EBITDA does FitHub need in year 5 for Summit to make 2.5×?
questions.answer:
Equity needed at exit = 2.5 × $100M = $250M. Add remaining debt $60M → enterprise value $310M.

At 8× → EBITDA needed = $310M ÷ 8 ≈ $38.75M, i.e. +$13.75M (+55%) from today's $25M.

questions.q: Management's plan has three parts. How much EBITDA does it add?

rows: Open 20 gyms by year 4; each makes $0.4M EBITDA when mature; costs $2M each to fit out
$25 → $27/month across all gyms; expect to lose 5% of members
LED lighting and solar panels: $2M a year saved
exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Management value creation plan

questions.q: What concerns would you raise with the investment committee?
questions.answer:
• Cash tension: the plan spends $40M on new gyms (20 × $2M) but also assumes debt falls by $40M from cash flow. Both need the same cash, so check it's possible to do both.
  • Exit multiple: if it drops to 7×: EV = 7 × 38.1 ≈ $267M → equity $207M → ~2.1×.
  • Price rise: budget customers are price-sensitive; competitors may not follow.
  • New gyms take time to fill; year-4 openings may not be mature by the exit.
questions.note: Candidates who spot the cash tension without being prompted are at offer level.

reco: At $200M, FitHub returns about 2.45× in our base case, just short of the 2.5× target, with real downside if exit multiples fall or the cash plan doesn't hold together. I'd recommend Summit bids, but at around $190M (7.6×). Keeping $100M of debt, Summit's equity falls to $90M, and the same plan returns ~2.7× ($245M ÷ $90M). The conditions: a funded capex plan for the new gyms and a price test in 10 gyms before the rise goes everywhere. If the seller won't move, walk away.
great: Works backwards from the return to the EBITDA needed
Gives returns as a multiple and checks them
Spots the capex vs debt-paydown cash conflict
Recommends a price, not just yes or no

title: CloudLedger
sub: How should a software company price its new AI add-on?
skills: Value-based pricing · price-volume trade-off · portfolio effects
prompt: CloudLedger sells online accounting software to 200,000 small businesses at $50 a month. It has built an AI add-on that does routine bookkeeping automatically. The product team wants to know what to charge for it.

clarify.a: Maximise profit from the add-on, but the CEO also cares about keeping core customers.
About $15 per customer per month (mostly AI computing).
A standalone AI bookkeeping tool costs $99/month. A part-time bookkeeper costs ~$40/hour.
Optional add-on on top of the $50 plan.

structure.root: What price for the AI add-on?

hypothesis: The value to customers is far above the cost, so the price will sit between the competitor's $99 and a much lower adoption-friendly price. The trade-off between margin and adoption is the real question.

questions.q: What is the add-on worth to a typical customer?
questions.answer: The add-on saves about 6 hours of bookkeeping a month (from pilot data). 6 × $40 = $240/month of value. Cost to serve is $15, and the competitor charges $99. So-what: the sensible range is roughly $30-$100. Pricing at the full $240 value isn't realistic: customers expect to keep some of the saving.
questions.note: Give the '6 hours' figure if the candidate asks how much time it saves.

questions.q: A customer survey shows how many would buy at each price. Which price maximises add-on profit?
questions.answer:
Annual profit = 200,000 × adoption × (price − $15) × 12

$2980k × $14 × 12 = $13.4M
$4960k × $34 × 12 = $24.5M
$7936k × $64 × 12 = $27.6M
$9920k × $84 × 12 = $20.2M

$79 maximises add-on profit (~$27.6M a year).

questions.q: New data: customers who use the add-on are far less likely to cancel CloudLedger. Each adopter is worth an extra $200 a year of core-product profit. Does this change your answer?
questions.answer:
Add $200 × adopters to each option:

$2913.4 + 16.0 = $29.4M
$4924.5 + 12.0 = $36.5M
$7927.6 + 7.2 = $34.8M
$9920.2 + 4.0 = $24.2M

$49 now wins. Looking at the whole customer, not just the add-on, changes the answer. So-what: price for adoption, because the add-on's biggest value is keeping core customers.

reco: Launch the AI add-on at $49 a month. On its own the add-on would make the most at $79, but each adopter is also much less likely to cancel, which makes $49 about $1.6M a year better overall (≈$36.5M vs $34.8M). Consider a 'Pro' tier at ~$89 later for heavier users. Risk: AI computing costs could rise with usage. Next step: A/B test $49 vs $59 with new customers.
great: Uses all three pricing lenses before the survey
Calculates profit, not revenue
Changes the answer when new data arrives, and says why

title: FreshMart
sub: A hard discounter is coming. How should a regional grocer respond?
skills: Sizing the threat · comparing responses to doing nothing
prompt: FreshMart operates 60 supermarkets in the US Midwest. A European hard discounter (small stores, ~1,500 products, prices 20-30% below supermarkets) has announced 25 new stores in FreshMart's region over the next three years. FreshMart's CEO wants a plan to respond.

clarify.a: Average store sells $20M a year; EBIT margin 4%. Contribution on each lost dollar of sales ≈ 25%.
30 of FreshMart's 60 stores are within 3 miles of a planned discounter store.
In other regions, supermarkets near a new discounter lost ~12% of sales in year 1 and ~8% for good.
Strong fresh food, local brand, good service; prices ~10% above market average.

hypothesis: The threat is concentrated in half the stores, so a targeted response probably beats a chain-wide price cut.

questions.q: How much profit is at risk if FreshMart does nothing?
questions.answer:
Sales lost for good = 30 stores × $20M × 8% = $48M/year. Profit lost = $48M × 25% = $12M/year.

Total EBIT = 60 × $20M × 4% = $48M → doing nothing costs a quarter of FreshMart's profit.

questions.q: Which customers leave? Look at this exhibit.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Sales lost by category at supermarkets near a discounter (other regions)

questions.answer: Losses concentrate in packaged groceries and household goods (13-14%), where products are identical and price wins. Fresh categories barely move (2-3%). So-what: fight on price only for packaged staples, and lean into fresh, where FreshMart is stronger.

questions.q: Option A: match the discounter's prices on 300 key packaged items in the 30 exposed stores. That gives up 3 margin points on 20% of their sales, and halves the sustained sales loss (8% → 4%). Worth it?
questions.answer:
Cost = 30 × $20M × 20% × 3% = $3.6M/year. Benefit = sales loss falls by 4% → 30 × $20M × 4% × 25% = $6.0M/year saved.

Net +$2.4M vs doing nothing. Remaining damage ≈ −12 + 6 − 3.6 = −$9.6M. Price matching helps, but it isn't enough on its own.

questions.q: What else should FreshMart do?
questions.answer:
• Private label on packaged staples: discounter-level prices at better margins
  • Double down on fresh: bigger produce and deli counters in exposed stores; the discounter's range is thin here
  • Loyalty programme with personalised offers to keep high-value families
  • Don't cut prices chain-wide: 30 unaffected stores would give away margin for nothing

reco: Doing nothing puts $12M a year at risk, about a quarter of FreshMart's profit. Respond in the 30 exposed stores only: match prices on ~300 packaged staples (net +$2.4M), launch a private-label range in the same categories, and invest in fresh food, where the discounter is weak and customers don't leave. Avoid a chain-wide price war. Next step: pilot the full package in the first 5 stores the discounter targets, and track weekly sales by category.
great: Compares every option against doing nothing
Uses the category chart to decide where to fight
Keeps the response limited to the stores that are actually exposed

title: Desert Dairy
sub: Should a dairy company build a new plant?
skills: Demand vs capacity · timing · cheaper alternatives first
prompt: Desert Dairy is a leading dairy producer in Saudi Arabia. Its one plant can produce 500 million litres a year and is running at 460M litres. Demand is growing ~7% a year. The board is considering a new $150M plant that would add 200M litres of capacity. Should they build it?

clarify.a: Contribution ≈ $0.30 per litre.
About 3 years from decision to production.
Engineers say $20M of upgrades could squeeze 60M more litres from the existing plant within a year.
Two competitors have also announced expansions.

hypothesis: They will need more capacity, but the cheap upgrade should come first. The real question is when to commit to the new plant, given the 3-year build.

questions.q: When does Desert Dairy run out of capacity?
questions.answer:
Year012345
Demand (M litres, +7%/yr)460492527564603645

Current plant (500M) runs out in year 2. With the $20M upgrade (560M) it's enough until year 3, when demand reaches 564M. A new plant takes 3 years, so the decision has to be made now to have capacity by year 3-4.

questions.q: Is the $20M upgrade worth it?
questions.answer: Extra volume sold: year 2 ≈ 27M litres (527 − 500) → $8M; year 3 onwards the full 60M litres → $18M/yr. Payback ≈ 2 years. Easily worth it, and it buys time.

questions.q: Here is the industry picture. Does this change anything?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Saudi dairy capacity vs demand, billion litres (case data)
exhibit.note: Includes competitors' announced expansions, but not Desert Dairy's new plant.

questions.answer: Industry capacity grows 25% while demand grows ~23%. Utilisation is ~87% today and stays ~85% in three years even before our plant. Adding 0.2bn more would push it to ~81%. So-what: more capacity → pressure on prices. Model a lower contribution (e.g. $0.25/litre) for the new plant's volume, and consider building it in phases.

reco: Do the $20M upgrade immediately: it pays back in about 2 years and covers demand until year 3. Approve the new plant now because of the 3-year build, but in two phases (e.g. 100M litres first), because competitors are also expanding and prices may come under pressure. Use co-packers to cover any short-term peaks. Next steps: firm up raw-milk supply contracts, and rerun the plant economics at $0.25/litre.
great: Builds the demand table year by year
Spots that the 3-year build forces the decision now
Tries the cheaper option first
Considers competitor supply and prices, not only our own demand

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Days per stage of a heavy check

questions.answer: Repair time is the same (10 days). The gap is all waiting: parts (9 vs 2 days) and approvals (3 vs 1). SkyLine spends 12 of its 28 days (43%) waiting. (Best airlines spend one extra day on testing.) So-what: this is a planning problem, not a skills problem. Fix parts first: it's 7 of the 8 days.

questions.q: The team proposes: (1) order parts in advance based on past checks, holding $5M of extra stock (cost of holding stock: 20% a year); (2) digital sign-off software at $0.5M a year. Parts waiting falls to 4 days and approvals to 1. Is it worth it?
questions.answer:
Days saved = (9 − 4) + (3 − 1) = 7 days → 7 × 20 × $60k = $8.4M/year.

Costs = $5M × 20% + $0.5M = $1.5M/year. Net ≈ +$6.9M/year. Clearly worth it.

reco: SkyLine's heavy checks take 8 days longer than the best airlines because aircraft wait for parts and approvals, not because repairs are slow. Pre-ordering parts and digital sign-off cut 7 days per check, worth $8.4M a year for $1.5M of cost (net ~$6.9M). Start with the next 5 checks, then look at the testing stage, where SkyLine is actually faster than its peers. Risk: holding parts that don't get used, so review the parts list every quarter.
great: Sizes the prize first
Separates working time from waiting time
Nets off the cost of holding stock

title: Visit Al Noor
sub: How can a Gulf state double its international tourists?
prompt: The tourism authority of Al Noor, a (fictional) Gulf state, receives 5 million international visitors a year. As part of its plan to diversify the economy away from oil, the government wants 10 million visitors a year by 2033 (7 years from now). The minister has asked us what it would take.

clarify.a: Jobs for nationals, foreign currency, less dependence on oil revenue.
GCC neighbours 40%, Europe 25%, South Asia 20%, others 15%.
35,000 hotel rooms, ~70% occupancy. 80% of visitors stay in hotels for 4 nights on average, 1.8 guests per room.
12,000 rooms under construction or approved.

structure.root: What does it take to reach 10M visitors?

hypothesis: Doubling in 7 years needs ~10% growth a year. That's hard but doable. I suspect hotel capacity and flights, not demand, will be the bottleneck.

questions.q: What annual growth rate is needed?
questions.answer: (10 ÷ 5)^(1/7) − 1 ≈ 10.4% a year. Rule of 72 check: 72 ÷ 10.4 ≈ 7 years to double. ✓

questions.q: How many hotel rooms will Al Noor need for 10M visitors? Assume a healthy target occupancy of 75%.
questions.answer:
Guest-nights = 10M × 80% × 4 = 32M → room-nights = 32M ÷ 1.8 ≈ 17.8M.

Rooms = 17.8M ÷ (365 × 75%) ≈ 65,000 rooms. Today 35,000 + 12,000 pipeline = 47,000 → shortfall ≈ 18,000 rooms.

Sanity check on today: 5M × 0.8 × 4 ÷ 1.8 ≈ 8.9M room-nights ÷ (35,000 × 365) ≈ 70% occupancy. ✓ matches the data.

questions.q: Air capacity is the other constraint. What do you conclude?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Visitors by source market, millions
exhibit.note: Growth potential = analyst estimate of extra visitors by 2033 with better flights and visas.

questions.answer: Potential growth totals ~5.0M, just enough for the 10M target, with Europe and South Asia making up ~70% of it. These are long-haul and flight-dependent: new routes and airline deals are critical. GCC visitors mostly drive, so they don't need flights.

questions.q: What should the government do, and what should it leave to the private sector?
questions.answer:
• Government: e-visa / visa on arrival for priority markets; incentives for airlines on new routes; airport capacity; an events calendar; training nationals for hospitality jobs
  • Private sector: build the 18,000 extra rooms (land or tax incentives to attract them); attractions; tour operators
  • Both: sustainability standards (water, energy) and protecting the culture that attracts visitors

reco: Reaching 10 million visitors by 2033 needs ~10% growth a year, and the binding constraints are capacity, not demand. Al Noor needs ~65,000 hotel rooms, about 18,000 beyond today's pipeline, and new flight routes from Europe and South Asia, which offer ~70% of the growth. I recommend that government focuses on visas, airline route deals, events and a national workforce programme, and uses land and tax incentives to bring in private hotel investment. Next step: a joint plan with the national airline for 10 new routes.
great: Converts visitors into rooms correctly
Checks the model against today's 70% occupancy
Separates public and private roles
Links tourism to the government's real goal (jobs, diversification)

title: Plugged In
sub: How big is the UK market for home EV chargers?
prompt: A private equity fund is looking at a company that installs electric-vehicle chargers in people's homes. Before going further, they want a quick estimate: how many home chargers are installed in the UK each year, and what is that worth?

clarify.a: Home chargers only (not public or workplace). Units per year and $ value including installation.
None given. The candidate should make sensible assumptions and say them out loud.

branches.head: Used EV buyers
items: Used EVs bought by first-time EV owners

hypothesis: I'd guess a few hundred thousand units a year, worth a few hundred million dollars.

questions.q: Walk me through your estimate.
questions.answer:
These are illustrative assumptions a candidate might use. They're there to show the method, not to be quoted as facts.

New cars sold in the UK per year~1.9M
× share that are fully electric~25% → ~475k
× have a driveway or garage~60% → ~285k
× install a charger~80% → ~230k
+ first-time EV owners buying used (~200k × 60% × 50%)~60k
+ replacements (early market)small
Total units per year~290k
× ~$1,000 installed≈ $290M

questions.q: How would you sanity-check this?
questions.answer:
• Supply side: number of installers × jobs per installer per year
  • Cross-check: ~80% of new-EV owners with parking install one, so units should track EV sales closely
  • Ask for the limiting factor: in many cities, off-street parking (not demand) limits the market

reco: Roughly 290,000 home chargers a year, worth about $300M, driven mainly by new EV sales and limited by how many people have off-street parking. For the fund the growth story matters more than the level: the market grows in line with EV adoption, and the biggest upside is the ~40% of households without driveways, if kerbside solutions emerge.
great: States a guess before calculating
Segments new vs used buyers
Names the limiting factor (parking)
Rounds sensibly and gives one clear number

title: SnackCo Protein Bar
sub: Should a snack maker launch a protein bar?
prompt: SnackCo is a mid-sized snack company best known for its granola bars. Its marketing team wants to launch a high-protein bar for gym-goers. Launch costs are $12M in the first year. Should SnackCo launch?

clarify.a: Sells to retailers at $1.50 per bar; variable cost $0.70.
$8M marketing + $4M production line, all in year 1.
Break even in year 1, or at least show a clear path to it.

hypothesis: The margin per bar is healthy. The risk is volume: whether SnackCo can sell enough bars in year 1 to cover $12M.

questions.q: How many bars does SnackCo need to sell to break even in year 1?
questions.answer: Contribution = $1.50 − $0.70 = $0.80. Breakeven = $12M ÷ $0.80 = 15M bars.

questions.q: Research says 20% of protein-bar buyers would otherwise have bought a SnackCo granola bar (contribution $0.50). Does that change the answer?
questions.answer: Effective contribution = $0.80 − 20% × $0.50 = $0.70. Breakeven = $12M ÷ $0.70 ≈ 17.1M bars.

questions.q: Is 17M bars achievable? Here is the market data.

rows: Regular buyers in SnackCo's retail channels
Bars bought per buyer per week
Realistic year-1 share for a new brand
exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Market data (case data)

questions.answer:
Market = 2M × 1.5 × 52 = 156M bars/year. At 10% share → 15.6M bars.

That just covers the 15M breakeven, but falls short of the 17.1M needed once cannibalisation is included → year-1 loss ≈ (17.1 − 15.6) × $0.70 ≈ $1M.

So-what: close to breakeven. The launch is attractive if year 2 continues without the $4M line cost, but year 1 is borderline.

reco: Launch, but test before committing the full $8M marketing budget. Once granola-bar cannibalisation is counted, SnackCo needs ~17M bars to break even in year 1, and a realistic 10% share gives ~15.6M, a small loss of about $1M. Year 2 is profitable since the $4M line is a one-off. Start in two regions with gym and fitness-retail partners, measure repeat purchase, then scale. Risk: big protein brands discounting to defend shelf space.
great: Includes cannibalisation in the breakeven
Converts a share into bars and compares with breakeven
Notices the one-off cost makes year 2 different

title: Vertex Mobile
sub: Why is a telecom operator's revenue falling?
skills: Isolating the problem · segmenting · flanker brands
prompt: Vertex is the second-largest mobile operator in its country. Revenue has fallen 6% in a year, from about $2.12B to $1.99B, while costs are flat. The CEO wants to know what's going on and what to do.

clarify.a: Postpaid (monthly contracts) and prepaid (pay-as-you-go). No big enterprise or fixed-line business.
Market revenue is flat overall, so Vertex is losing share.
A competitor launched 'Zap', a digital-only prepaid brand: unlimited data for $15/month, sold only via an app.

hypothesis: The new $15 digital brand is the obvious suspect. I'd expect the loss to be in prepaid, among young, data-heavy users.

questions.q: Here's revenue by stream. Where is the drop?
questions.answer: Postpaid is flat. All of the drop is prepaid (−$127M, −18%): subscribers −14% (5.0M → 4.3M) and revenue per user −4%. Losing customers matters about three times more than lower revenue per user.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 2 · Prepaid churn (% of customers leaving per month) by age

questions.answer: Churn among 18-25s jumped from 3% to 8% a month; other ages barely moved. Young, digital, data-hungry users are leaving, almost certainly for Zap. So-what: this is a targeted competitive attack, not a general problem with Vertex.

questions.q: Vertex could launch its own digital brand at $15. It expects to win back 400,000 subscribers, but ~2% of its 3.3M postpaid customers (paying $35/month) might switch down to it. Net effect?
questions.answer:
Gain = 400k × $15 × 12 = +$72M/year. Loss = 2% × 3.3M ≈ 67k × ($35 − $15) × 12 ≈ −$16M/year.

Net ≈ +$56M/year, recovering ~45% of the lost revenue. A digital brand is also cheaper to run (no shops).

reco: Vertex's revenue drop is entirely in prepaid, driven by 18-25 year-olds leaving for a competitor's $15 digital brand. I recommend launching Vertex's own digital-only brand at a similar price. It recovers ~$56M a year net of postpaid customers switching down. Keep it clearly separate from postpaid (app-only, no handset deals) to limit switching. Next steps: a 3-month launch plan, and a retention offer for young prepaid users whose contracts are ending.
great: Isolates the stream before diagnosing
Splits subscribers vs revenue per user
Includes postpaid customers switching down in the maths

title: RideNow Drivers
sub: Design a feature to keep ride-hailing drivers on the platform
skills: Two-sided platforms · user segmentation · prioritisation · metrics
prompt: You're a product manager at RideNow, a ride-hailing app. Many new drivers quit within their first 90 days, which forces RideNow to keep spending on recruiting. Design a product feature to improve driver retention.

clarify.a: About 50% of new drivers stop driving within 90 days.
Your choice. Pick one and say why.
Must be live in one quarter. Can't simply raise pay across the board.

structure.root: A feature to keep new drivers

branches.head: Goal & users
items: Segments: full-time, part-time, students, new arrivals

hypothesis: New part-time drivers quit because they can't predict what they'll earn. A feature that shows them when and where to drive will have the biggest impact.

questions.q: Which driver segment would you focus on, and why?
questions.answer: New part-time drivers (drive <20 hours/week). They're the biggest group of quitters and the most flexible about when they drive. Full-timers already learn the patterns. Remember that RideNow is a two-sided platform: riders benefit too when more drivers stay at peak times.

questions.q: List the pain points and pick a solution.
questions.answer:
Pain pointSolutionImpact / effort
Don't know when to drive to earn wellWeekly 'earnings planner' showing best hours and expected $/hourHigh / Medium
Long empty time between ridesLive demand heatmapMedium / Low
One bad rating early hurts a lotRating protection for the first 20 tripsMedium / Low
No one to askMentor matching with experienced driversMedium / High

Pick: the earnings planner. It goes straight at the main reason people quit (uncertain earnings) and can be built from data RideNow already has.

questions.q: How would you measure success?
questions.answer:
• North star: % of new drivers still active at day 90
  • Inputs: % of new drivers using the planner weekly; hours driven in planned peak slots; earnings per hour in weeks 1-4
  • Guardrails: rider waiting times (if all drivers chase the same peaks, other times suffer); earnings of existing drivers

reco: Build a weekly earnings planner for new part-time drivers: it shows the best hours and areas to drive, with expected earnings per hour. It tackles the main reason drivers quit, unpredictable earnings, and uses data RideNow already has. Measure success by 90-day driver retention, with rider waiting times as a guardrail. Launch to half of new drivers in one city as an A/B test, then expand.
great: Lays out the plan of the answer up front
Segments drivers and picks one group with a reason
Remembers the platform has two sides
Gives a north star, inputs and a guardrail, not a list of ten metrics

title: LinguaLeap
sub: Weekly users of a language app fell 8%. Why?
prompt: You're a product manager at LinguaLeap, a language-learning app. This morning the dashboard shows weekly active users (WAU) down 8% compared with last week. Your boss asks you to find out why.

clarify.a: Users who complete at least one lesson in 7 days. Definition unchanged.
Sudden: WAU was stable for months, then dropped over 4-5 days.
No holiday this week; last year the same week was flat.

hypothesis: A sudden drop with no season to explain it usually means something we changed. I'd segment by platform and check recent releases first.

questions.q: Here's WAU by platform. What's going on?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · WAU index by platform (Week −4 = 100)
exhibit.note: Android app version 5.2 was released at the start of this week. Android = ~45% of users.

questions.answer: iOS is flat. Android fell ~18% (45% of users × 18% ≈ 8% overall ✓). It started the same week as Android release 5.2. So-what: almost certainly caused by the release, not by users or competitors.

questions.q: What would you check next?
questions.answer:
• Crash rate and app-start success on 5.2
  • Push notification delivery: lesson reminders bring back many users; a change in permissions could silently stop them
  • Funnel: open app → start lesson → finish lesson, to see where Android users drop

Interviewer reveals: reminder notifications delivered on Android fell from 92% to 15% after 5.2, because a new permission prompt is declined by most users.

questions.q: What do you do now?
questions.answer:
• Now: hotfix that asks for the permission at a better moment, with a clear explanation (e.g. after the user's first lesson streak)
  • Recover: email/in-app message to affected users to switch reminders back on
  • Prevent: add 'notifications delivered' to release checklists and alerts

reco: The 8% drop is an Android problem caused by release 5.2: a new notification permission is being declined, so reminders no longer reach most users and fewer come back for lessons. Ship a hotfix that asks for the permission at a better moment, win back affected users by email, and add notification delivery to the release checklist so it can't happen silently again.
great: Checks data and definitions first
Segments before guessing
Confirms the size (45% × 18% ≈ 8%)
Fixes now and prevents it happening again
